title: Node memory slab bloat triage notes
summary: On 2024-10-12 we observed repeated node-level memory pressure on a subset of GKE nodes leading to large eviction waves. Initial signal pointed to slab growth (kernel slab caches) rather than user-space RSS. This doc captures timeline, quick mitigations used on-call, hypotheses, diagnostic commands, and recommended postmortem follow-ups and runbook edits.
content:
Context:
- Cluster: prod-eu-west-1 (mixed n1-highmem + custom GPU pools).
- Impact: ~12% of pods in customer-facing namespaces restarted over ~45 minutes due to NodeOOM and eviction pressure; p99 latency spikes for API frontends.
- Notable: top memory consumers by container RSS were normal; node free memory dropped while process RSS stayed flat.

Detection timeline (approx):
- 08:41 UTC: paging alerts from monitoring (node mem.available < 15%) for nodes pool-gpu-03..05
- 08:45 UTC: kubelet reporting eviction thresholds crossed, start of Pod eviction flurry.
- 08:47 UTC: Pager triggers. SRE on-call begins triage.
- 08:50 UTC: Top-level dashboards show kube-apiserver p99 spike; many pods in CrashLoopBackOff.
- 09:10 UTC: Short-term mitigations applied (see below).

Quick on-call diagnostic checks executed: (commands are approximate examples used during triage)
- kubectl get nodes -o wide --show-labels | grep pool-gpu-03
- ssh node (gcloud compute ssh)
- free -m; cat /proc/meminfo | egrep 'MemAvailable|Slab|SReclaimable|SUnreclaim'
- slabtop -o --sort=slab
- ps aux --sort=-rss | head -n 30
- crictl stats | jq -r '.containers[] | [.name, .memory.rss] | @tsv'

Findings during triage:
- MemAvailable low (~200MB) but aggregate process RSS accounted for < 40% of used memory.
- /proc/meminfo showed Slab and SReclaimable growing quickly; SUnreclaim was large.
- slabtop indicated growth in dentry, inode_cache, and a lesser amount in nf_conntrack (surprising given network load).
- no recent deployments to explain a sudden new in-kernel allocator pressure.
- kubelet kube-proxy and cni plugins not showing obvious leaks in user-space.

Immediate mitigation performed (to protect customer traffic):
1) Cordoned the three affected nodes to stop new pods from scheduling (kubectl cordon node-XXX).
2) Drained non-critical pods with --ignore-daemonsets --delete-local-data; prioritized keeping stateful/critical control-plane pods.
3) Added temporary node-pool capacity: scaled up pool-gpu by 4 nodes to absorb load and allow evicted pods to reschedule.
4) Disabled a candidate kernel module on a small test node (nf_conntrack debug off) to see effect; not rolled cluster-wide.
5) Tuned kubelet eviction thresholds in the nodegroup autoscaling template (lowered imagefs and nodefs thresholds by 5%) as a short stopgap.

Short-term outcome:
- After cordon+drain+scale, pod restarts rate decreased and p99 latency returned toward baseline within ~22 minutes.
- Slab counters on the cordoned nodes continued to grow for a bit, then slowly stabilized on nodes that were rebooted.

Hypotheses (ranked):
A) Kernel slab allocator leak triggered by a workload-specific kernel interaction (e.g., heavy file churn, fuse, or high metadata ops) causing dentry/inode caches to grow and not be reclaimed quickly.
B) A miscompiled kernel/CNI module or a regression in a kernel patch (we recently rolled a host kernel update to this node pool 36 hours prior).
C) nf_conntrack hash resizing due to bursty external connections (unlikely as conntrack counters didn't show massive opens).
D) Userspace process repeatedly creating/destroying large numbers of ephemeral files (e.g., tmpfs churn) — not ruled out.

Root-cause evidence to collect for postmortem:
- Full /proc/slabinfo snapshots over time for affected nodes (we captured at 08:46, 08:55, 09:05).
- dmesg/syslog around 36 hours before and during the incident to see kernel warnings.
- History of kernel package rollouts for the affected node pool (rollback timeline).
- Container-level file access patterns (inotify, fstat traces) for pods that were on affected nodes (if available).
- Probe kubelet logs for OOM/kubepods reaping messages.

Longer-term mitigations / action items (owner and ETA where assigned):
- (eng-sre) Add slabinfo time-series collection to node exporter (Grafana) and create alert rule for sustained slab growth > X MB over 10 min. ETA: 2024-11-01.
- (platform-engineering) Run kernel-rollback experiment on a small subset of nodes to confirm hypothesis B; coordinate with cloud infra. ETA: 2024-10-20.
- (applied-ml) Identify pods with heavy metadata ops: add optional sidecar instrumentation (ftrace/inotify) to suspect jobs and run in staging. ETA: 2024-10-28.
- (eng-sre) Update runbook (node-memory-pressure) to include slab-specific diagnostics (slabtop, /proc/slabinfo examples, recommend cordon+drain thresholds). ETA: 2024-10-18.
- (eng-sre) Add a KCS (known cause signature) entry for "kernel slab growth leading to eviction" with steps for quick isolation. ETA: 2024-10-22.

Runbook edits proposed (quick diff ideas):
- Add a new subsection "Detecting kernel slab pressure" with these signals: MemAvailable << expected, Slab/SReclaimable rising, slabtop dominated by dentry/inode, process RSS stable.
- Prescribed remediation order: cordon -> drain non-critical -> scale -> selective reboot -> kernel rollback.
- Commands to capture artifacts: (list exactly what to snapshot and where to upload)
  - sudo cat /proc/slabinfo > /tmp/slabinfo-{{node}}-{{timestamp}}
  - sudo slabtop -o -n 30 -d 2 > /tmp/slabtop-{{node}}-{{timestamp}}.txt
  - sudo dmesg --ctime --since "1 hour ago" > /tmp/dmesg-{{node}}-{{timestamp}}.log
  - kubectl get pod -o wide --field-selector spec.nodeName={{node}} > /tmp/pods-on-node-{{node}}.txt

Monitoring & alert tuning recommendations:
- Create a metric for slab_unreclaimable = Slab - SReclaimable and surface it. Alert if slab_unreclaimable > 1GB for 10min.
- Add multi-signal alert that combines MemAvailable drop + slab_unreclaimable growth to reduce noisy alerts for simple RSS spikes.

Open questions for investigation:
- Why did slab reclaim not kick in? Is there a kernel config or cgroup pressure preventing reclaim?
- Does our GKE node image include any custom modules that we added recently? (check agent & startup scripts)
- Could kubelet eviction tuning have accelerated visible impact (i.e., eviction thresholds too aggressive causing restarts before OS reclaim)?
- Any correlation between scheduled batch jobs (nightly model evals) and time windows where slab grew?

Communication notes (what we told stakeholders):
- Initial customer comms: "We observed transient node-level memory pressure affecting a subset of services; we cordoned nodes and scaled capacity; services are recovering. Investigating root cause and will follow up with postmortem."
- Internal: Standup at 10:30 UTC to sync with platform, applied-ml, and console teams.

Immediate follow-ups assigned during handoff:
- Marcus: collect and upload slab snapshots and dmesg logs to linked_artifacts confluence page. (done 2024-10-13)
- Samira: run controlled repro on staging with file-churn workload to see if dentry/inode caches behave similarly.
- Ravi: schedule kernel-rollback test with infra and capture metrics pre/post.

Notes / miscellaneous observations from on-call freeform:
- On one rebooted node slab reclaimed more quickly; suggests reboot kills whatever object was holding refs in kernel.
- I/O patterns for the pods on that node were heavy metadata reads (ls/scandir) from NFS-mounted volumes used by an internal testing job — this is a promising lead.
- conntrack counts were moderately high but not the primary driver.

TL;DR action summary (short):
- Symptoms: mem.available low, slab growth high, process RSS stable -> probable kernel slab bloat.
- Mitigation: cordon+drain affected nodes, scale up pool, selective reboots.
- Next: add slab metrics & alerts, repro in staging, kernel rollback experiment, update runbook.

End of notes.

(If you worked on this incident and have additional details, append to this doc with timestamps and links to artifact uploads.)
